vignette:
Here is a clinical vignette written from the perspective of a psychologist.

Patient: Mark, Age 46

Mark sits forward on the edge of the chair, his forearms resting on his knees. He’s a tall, lean man with a quiet intensity, dressed in a well-worn band t-shirt and dark jeans. He has a habit of rubbing his palms on his thighs as he speaks, a repetitive, grounding motion. He tells me he’s been a graphic designer for twenty years, working from a home studio that was once his sanctuary. Now, he can barely look at the screen.

The story comes out in fragments, each piece heavy with unspoken weight. It happened eight months ago, on a Tuesday night. Mark had been out late, finishing a freelance project at a coffee shop. He was driving home on a familiar two-lane road, the one that runs along the river. He saw the flashing lights in his rearview mirror—red and blue, strobing in the dark. His heart had jumped, a sudden, sharp spike of adrenaline. He’d done nothing wrong. He checked his speed. He was under the limit. He pulled over carefully, hands at ten and two, and killed the engine.

The officer’s flashlight was a blinding white star in his window. Mark rolled it down. He remembers the smell of the officer’s cologne—something cheap and cloying, like pine and cigarettes. The officer asked for his license and registration. Mark reached for the glovebox. That’s when the world shattered.

He doesn’t remember the exact sequence of sounds. A shout. A metallic click. A shattering of glass. The officer later claimed Mark had made a "furtive movement." Mark remembers the cold, hard muzzle of a gun pressed against his temple, the officer’s weight on his back as he was yanked from the car and slammed onto the asphalt. He remembers the gravel biting into his cheek, the taste of blood and dirt, the officer’s knee grinding into his spine. He remembers the voice, a disembodied roar in his ear: “Don’t you fucking move.”

He was handcuffed for twenty minutes before another unit arrived and the officer realized his mistake. A routine license plate check had flagged a car of the same make and color, but a different model year. Mark was released with a curt apology, a smudge of dirt on his face, and a crack in his soul that has only widened since.

Now, Mark’s studio is a tomb. He used to love the hum of his computer, the feel of a stylus in his hand, the quiet challenge of a blank canvas. Now, the sound of the cooling fan is the sound of a threat. A sudden notification on his phone—a text message chime—makes him flinch, his heart hammering against his ribs as if trying to escape his chest. He has stopped working on projects that require client calls. The sound of an unfamiliar male voice on the phone, especially one with a deep, authoritative tone, sends him into a cold sweat.

He cannot drive at night. The sight of a police cruiser in his peripheral vision—even parked, even empty—triggers a full-blown panic attack. His wife, Sarah, does all the grocery shopping now. He has become hypervigilant in his own home. He checks the locks on the doors three times before bed. He avoids the window that faces the street, a constant, anxious pull to look, to see if someone is watching. He flinches when Sarah touches him unexpectedly from behind.

The worst part, he tells me, is the shame. He is a grown man, a husband, a professional. He should be able to get over a traffic stop. He knows, intellectually, that he was the victim of a mistake, of a system that is broken. But the feeling in his body is not intellectual. It is a raw, animal terror that lives in his chest, a constant, low-level hum of dread.

Last week, he tried to go back to the coffee shop. He sat in the parking lot for ten minutes, his hands gripping the steering wheel, before he drove home, defeated. He hasn’t been able to work in three weeks. He spends most of his days in the basement, in the dark, scrolling through his phone on mute, waiting for the day to end. He looks at me with a hollow, exhausted expression. He doesn’t know how to get back to the person he was before the blue lights found him.
